source_evidence.anchor: a homogeneous first-order system ... in x and t
source_evidence.observation: The enclosing setting is a time-dependent, one-dimensional, homogeneous, first-order, constant-coefficient linear system q_t(x,t) + A q_x(x,t) = 0.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 23; printed page 1; paragraph following (1.1)
source_evidence.observation: The unknown is a real vector-valued function of space and time; A is a constant real m × m matrix. Subscripts denote partial derivatives with respect to t and x.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 23; printed page 1; scalar specialization paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: m = 1 and the matrix A reduces to a scalar value
source_evidence.observation: The simplest case is scalar and constant-coefficient. The text states that this problem is hyperbolic provided the scalar A is real.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 23; printed page 1; transport paragraph and (1.2)
source_evidence.anchor: one-dimensional pipe at constant velocity ū
source_evidence.observation: For a contaminant carried downstream by fluid moving at constant velocity ū, its concentration or density q(x,t) satisfies q_t(x,t) + ū q_x(x,t) = 0.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 23; printed page 1; (1.3) and adjoining sentences
source_evidence.observation: The text states that (1.2) admits solutions q(x,t) = q̃(x − ūt); the profile propagates at constant speed ū with unchanged shape.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 25; printed page 3; opening paragraph
source_evidence.anchor: real eigenvalues and a corresponding set of m linearly independent eigenvectors
source_evidence.observation: The enclosing definition of hyperbolicity for (1.1) requires real eigenvalues and a complete linearly independent set of eigenvectors; the eigenvalues give wave speeds.

source_evidence.anchor: where f(q) is the flux function
source_evidence.observation: The conservation-law setting is q_t + f(q)_x = 0, with integral balance d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)) for any two endpoints.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; paragraph following (1.10)
source_evidence.anchor: the flux function is f(q) = ūq
source_evidence.observation: The source identifies contaminant advection (1.2) with conservation of total contaminant mass and linear flux f(q) = ūq. Nonconservation, such as chemical reactions, requires source terms.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26; printed page 4; Section 1.1.2
source_evidence.anchor: provided that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth
source_evidence.observation: The differential conservation law follows from the integral form under sufficient smoothness. The text explicitly notes that many interesting solutions have discontinuities.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 27; printed page 5; Section 1.1.2 continuation
source_evidence.anchor: does not hold in the classical sense
source_evidence.observation: At a discontinuity in q the differential equation does not hold classically, whereas the integral conservation law continues to hold.

conclusions: The scalar constant-coefficient problem is hyperbolic provided its scalar coefficient is real. [Printed p. 1, scalar specialization paragraph.]

definitions_and_conventions: The subscripts t and x denote partial differentiation with respect to time and space. [Printed p. 1, paragraph following (1.1).]
Scalar means m = 1, so matrix multiplication in (1.1) specializes to scalar multiplication. [Printed p. 1, scalar specialization paragraph.]
Advective transport is a substance being carried along with fluid motion; (1.2) is called the advection equation in this context. [Printed p. 1, paragraphs introducing (1.2) and following (1.3).]
The transport flux is f(q) = ūq. The endpoint balance uses left-endpoint flux minus right-endpoint flux. [Printed p. 4, (1.10) and following paragraph.]

ambiguities.issue: The phrase 'for any function q̃' does not specify regularity or a solution concept.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed p. 1, following (1.3), says 'for any function'; printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2, requires sufficient smoothness for the differential derivation and rejects classical satisfaction at discontinuities.
ambiguities.impact: A precise classical statement needs regularity assumptions, while an integral or weak statement needs appropriate admissibility conditions. The passage does not select a precise function space.

ambiguities.issue: The inherited function domain includes all real times, while the motivating language describes time-dependent transport.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed p. 1 gives q : R × R → R^m after (1.1), and (1.2)–(1.3) introduce no restricted time interval.
ambiguities.impact: A restriction to nonnegative times would be an additional specialization rather than an explicit source requirement.

ambiguities.issue: The source calls ū both a velocity and a speed without imposing a sign convention.
ambiguities.evidence: Printed p. 1 introduces 'constant velocity ū' before (1.2) and describes propagation with 'constant speed ū' after (1.3).
ambiguities.impact: The formula fixes signed translation by ū. The terminology does not justify requiring ū > 0 or replacing ū with its absolute value in the equation.

contract_plain_english: In the one-dimensional real scalar specialization of the homogeneous constant-coefficient system, a real coefficient gives a hyperbolic problem. A conserved contaminant carried by fluid at constant velocity ū satisfies q_t + ūq_x = 0, and translated profiles q(x,t) = q̃(x − ūt) are presented as solutions whose shape remains unchanged. [Printed p. 1, (1.1)–(1.3) and adjoining paragraphs.] The associated conserved flux is f(q) = ūq. [Printed p. 4, following (1.10).] Although the profile is described as any function, the surrounding source distinguishes sufficiently smooth classical solutions from discontinuous solutions governed by integral conservation; it supplies no precise regularity class for this unrestricted wording. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2.]
